content.intro: File and stream operations cross a storage boundary. Check operation results, constrain paths, account for permissions and concurrent access, and validate uploads before they become trusted data. In this lesson, focus on reading files; then compare it with writing files. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use working with files when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: File and stream operations cross a storage boundary. Check operation results, constrain paths, account for permissions and concurrent access, and validate uploads before they become trusted data. For working with files, begin with reading files. Also distinguish writing files; appending content; file paths. content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Working with Files
content_blocks.code:
<?php
$file = tempnam(sys_get_temp_dir(), "php-course-");
if ($file === false) { throw new RuntimeException("Cannot create temp file"); }
file_put_contents($file, "ready\n");
echo trim((string) file_get_contents($file)) . PHP_EOL;
unlink($file);

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring a failed read or write.
common_mistakes.why: Partial or missing data can be mistaken for successful completion.
common_mistakes.fix: Check return values and throw or report a controlled error when required.

common_mistakes.why: Paths can escape the intended directory.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a controlled storage root and reject paths outside it.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting an uploaded filename or extension.
common_mistakes.why: Names and client-provided content types can be forged.
common_mistakes.fix: Generate storage names, enforce size/type policy, and isolate uploaded files.
